articles.title: 'Dukh hota hai': CWG gold medallist judoka Harsh Singh rues Asian Games snub
articles.summary: More sports News: NEW DELHI: âDukh hota hai. Mai iss bade chance ka wait kar rha tha par naam nahi aya [It hurts. I was waiting for this big opportunity, but my name di.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: âDukh hota hai. Mai iss bade chance ka wait kar rha tha par naam nahi aya [It hurts. I was waiting for this big opportunity, but my name didnât come up],â a dejected Harsh Singh told Timesofindia.com after being left out of the Indian judo squad for the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya.Just a month ago, Harsh made history as the first-ever male Indian judoka to win a gold medal at the Commonwealth Games 2026 in Glasgow in the menâs 60kg category.Although he did not meet the Asian Games selection criteria, he hoped his gold medal-winning performance would earn him a place in the squad. The 23-year-old believed his form and confidence after the Glasgow triumph could have helped him win another medal for India.India is going to send only three female judokas to the Asian Games - Asmita Dey, Women -48kg, Yamini Mourya - Women -57kg and Inunganbi Takhellambam - Women -70kg.What is the selection criteria?While top six in Asia via rankings was the operative standard set by SAI, in cases where judging by that marker was not possible or realistic, âa top-six finish among Asian nations in international competitionsâ, or a top-six finish at an Asian Championship would be the operative criterion.The ministry, in its release, however, added a relaxation clause: one that allowed it to choose an athlete for justifiable reasons, as recommended by experts from the concerned federation.Harsh did not meet either of the criteria, but his gold medal gave him hope of representing India at the mega event in Aichi-Nagoya.âI was told by the federation that my name was given and a total of 13 judokas names were given for Asian Games selection. I know that I didn't meet the criteria. But I was among the athletes who won the medals. I am in good touch, in form, in confidence, and I had the belief that I could win another medal for my country. But that's the life of an athlete I think,â Harsh said.Tough draw ended Asian Games hopesHarsh had a good opportunity to win an Asian Games berth when he participated in the Asian Championships, held in Ordos City, China, in April this year.As per the rules, judokas who won gold, silver or bronze medals, as well as those who fought in bronze-medal matches regardless of whether they won or lost, would qualify for the Asian Games.Unfortunately, Harsh got a tough draw and had to face Tokyo Olympics silver medallist Yang Yung-wei of Chinese Taipei. Harsh lost to Yang Yung-wei in the first round.Now, Harsh wants to leave this dejection behind and focus on the Lausanne Grand Slam.âWhen my name didnât appear on the list, I approached the federation. They said it was no longer in their hands and that nothing could be done now. I canât go to the Asian Games now, can I? So now Iâm focusing on the Lausanne Grand Slam,â he said.The electrician's son and his struggleFor years, Harsh had seen his father work as an electrician, going from home to home to repair switches, plugs, and electrical appliances in and around South West Delhiâs Dwarka locality. Whatever he earned was the livelihood of the family.The family also went through a difficult period and sometimes even struggled to arrange meals during the COVID-19 lockdown. With no one allowed to move around freely, work dried up. His father could no longer go from house to house. The daily earnings stopped completely. Sometimes it was Rs 500 to Rs 1000.The family's savings were exhausted. But despite all these tensions and worries, Harsh kept going.âAt that time, whatever little savings my father had, thatâs what we used to run the household on. That also ran out. We would borrow some money and somehow manage. But I never stopped my practice. I had decided that I had to do something for my family,â Harsh recalled.âIt was a very difficult time. Whatever savings we had were gone within two years because there were expenses for me as well. Sometimes I had to travel for competitions, and I had to maintain my diet. Even when there was no competition, we still had to maintain the same diet. So, basically, all our savings were exhausted,â he said.The turnaroundBut Harsh and his family didn't know that the struggles of his family would soon be over. The fortunes started changing within three years when Harsh won gold at the Nationals in 2024.The gold medal at the Nationals earned him a job in ITBP. After spending around eight to nine months there, Harsh received an offer from the Indian Army. He left ITBP and joined the Army as a Havaldar.âThe Indian Army has helped me a lot. Our Commandant and all the coaches, Roop Chand sir and Chandan sir, have supported me a lot. They told me, âYou focus on judo, we will take care of the rest.â The Army has said that I donât have to worry about doing a regular job while training. They have also helped by providing all the facilities and requirements, including my diet and supplements,â Harsh said.The life-changing CWG goldGlasgow brought the biggest moment of his career. For him, the CWG gold not only earned him a promotion in the Indian Army but also brought respect to his family.âThis is my first medal at the Commonwealth Games, and it is also my first international medal. This medal means a lot to me. This success is a very big thing for my family. I canât thank God enough. This medal is for my father and mother,â Harsh said.âNow, even the neighbours who didnât used to speak to us come to our house, meet my mother and father and have tea. For me, the most important thing is the respect my family has received,â he said.âI have told my father, âNow you rest and enjoy your life.â He has done a lot for me. I have seen him worried many times, but he never gave up. It is my turn now to do something for him and give him a relaxed life,â Harsh signed off.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Jonny Lomax: St Helens legend to retire at end of 2026 Super League season
articles.summary: Jonny Lomax has made 388 appearances for St Helens, winning five Grand Finals, one Challenge Cup and a World Club Challenge; he earned four caps for Great Britain and 11 for England, which included a World Cup final appearance against Australia in 2017
articles.body:
Lomax, who has not featured since fracturing his jaw in Saints' defeat by Warrington Wolves in June, has made 388 appearances for the club, winning five Grand Finals, one Challenge Cup and a World Club Challenge.

He won four caps for Great Britain and 11 for England, which included a World Cup final appearance against Australia in 2017.

Lomax confirmed the move with a post on his Instagram that read: "At the end of 2026, I will call time on my playing career. This was something I always planned, and those closest to me have always been aware of.

"Over the last 20 years [18 professionally], I have been able to live out a boyhood dream. Achieving far more than I could ever have imagined. Representing and captaining my hometown club and, of course, the pinnacle, representing England and Great Britain.

"I will retire at the age of 36, grateful for the life the game has given me, knowing I have given it everything I could, with the scars to prove it [19 operations, including 12 knee ops by the age of 26]. Despite this, I still feel lucky.

"For those that have supported me throughout it all... I hope I have been able to do you proud."

Saints are currently on 28 points and seventh in the Super League standings, one place outside of the play-off positions with three games to go.

They need to leapfrog one of Hull KR (sixth, 30 points), Leigh Leopards (fifth, 32 points) or Wakefield Trinity (fourth, 32 points) down the stretch.

Current Super League leaders Leeds Rhinos, as well as Wigan Warriors - tied on 38 points but with an inferior point differential - and Warrington Wolves, two back in third, have already qualified for the play-offs.

Sky Sports will show every game of the Super League live this season, including two matches each round exclusively live. The remaining five matches will be broadcast on Sky Sports+ .

articles.summary: Star pair lost to Cobolli and Bencic, who will play married partners Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils in the semifinal.

The return of Serena Williams to Arthur Ashe Stadium came to an abrupt end as she and Carlos Alcaraz fell 5-4(4), 4-1 to Flavio Cobolli and Belinda Bencic in the US Open mixed doubles quarterfinal, their magic fading after an inspired early performance.

The 23-time major winner had not competed at the crown jewel of US tennis since her tearful farewell from the sport in 2022, and fans erupted in deafening cheers as their queen took the court again on Tuesday.

The 44-year-old Williams had an easy rapport with Alcaraz, who is 21 years her junior, as the partners grinned and giggled their way past Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3, 4-1 in the opening round earlier on Tuesday.

But their firepower was extinguished by the ice-cold Cobolli and Bencic, who will play married partners Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils in a semifinal on Wednesday.

“Playing Serena and Carlos on Arthur Ashe is not easy. I was tired before the match, I’m tired now,” said the Italian Cobolli.

Williams, who is not competing in the singles, showed glimpses of her old brilliance in their opening match against Routliffe and Glasspool, blasting a 120mph (193.1km/h) ace to audible gasps from the packed house a little more than two months after she announced her stunning comeback .

Alcaraz, who has not played since April due to injury, shook off the early rust to close out the set with a forehand winner before they sprinted through the second set, embracing after the win in their matching royal purple outfits.

“It’s always such an amazing place to be here,” said Williams. “I never expected to be back on this court.”

The Roland Garros runner-up Cobolli and Tokyo Olympic champion Bencic were too tough a task, however, as Williams and Alcaraz made early mistakes and Cobolli sealed the tie-break with an ace.

The Swiss-Italian pair only upped their level from there, with no unforced errors in the second set, and gave credit to their opponents after the match.

“I don’t know how I landed on this court — to play Carlos and Serena is a great honour,” said Bencic.

The mixed doubles main draw kicked off in the second year of its revamped format, which put singles stars in the spotlight in an effort to lure more fans in a standalone spot the week before the singles main draw.

The move proved a commercial success in its debut year, drawing sellout crowds and attracting many of the sport’s biggest singles names despite criticism from some doubles specialists, who argued it marginalised established pairings.

Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka were beaten 1-4, 4-2, 10-2 by experienced doubles players Henry Patten and Katerina Siniakova in round one, with Siniakova sealing the upset in style with an ace.

Patten and Siniakova went on to lose to Monfils and Svitolina in the quarters 5-4(6), 4-5(3), 10-8 in their second match of the day.

“The chemistry is what put us through because we understand each other even by the look at each other’s reaction or kind of mood,” said Svitolina. “We can find the right words for each other.”

Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik will play Russian pair Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev in the other semifinal on Wednesday.

Rublev and Andreeva beat last year’s champions, Italian duo Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori, 1-4, 4-1, 11-9 in the opening round before ousting Casper Ruud and Diana Shnaider 4-1, 4-5(9), 10-5.

Five-time US Open champion Roger Federer returned to the Arthur Ashe Stadium to play one last match for fun against longtime rival and friend Andy Roddick.

The event, billed as “An Icon Returns to New York”, packed the stands full of fans there to watch the 45-year-old from Switzerland face Roddick in a prime-time exhibition. Many wore hats with the distinctive “RF” logo that became commonplace in the sport during Federer’s decade and a half of dominance, featuring 20 Grand Slam titles.

“It’s great to be back in New York,” Federer said. “I have incredible memories, obviously, of this court, of the fans here, of the city.”

Federer reminisced about visiting for the first time to play juniors in 1998 and reaching the final. Three years later, his debut on centre court was a straight-sets loss to Andre Agassi.

Federer, who last competed at the US Open in 2019 and retired in 2022, then teamed up with John McEnroe and faced Roddick and Agassi in a doubles exhibition.

articles.title: Saffron Cresswell on life-changing accident and new career in para-canoe
articles.summary: Saffron Cresswell was a promising eventer before a fall left her paralysed. Just eight months after first sitting in a canoe, she is heading to the Worlds.
articles.body:
After four months in hospital, Saffron Cresswell was dreading coming home.

Before she had the fall that would leave her paralysed at the age of 23, she had 25 horses that she trained and rode in a business she had been running since she was 15 and was a talented eventer on a pathway towards the Olympics.

Eight years earlier her parents had sold their house to buy a yard to support her career, with the family living in two tiny touring caravans for six years before they converted part of a barn into a home.

For years, Cresswell had been up at 5am, riding four ponies before school, then more afterwards - if she even went in. She puts her school attendance at "68% or something ridiculous" because she was "so busy riding".

'Busy' in fact turns out to be a common theme with Cresswell. During rehab at the hospital, she'd be waiting outside the gym for it to open so she could get an hour in before her physio session was even due to start.

There had only been five days during the four months where she hadn't had a visitor and so when she finally returned home to Worcestershire, where the horses had all been sold, reality was anything but hectic.

"I came home and fundamentally the next day, both my parents went out the door and went to work," says the now 25-year-old Cresswell. "So, I was home alone in a house that I couldn't really get out of and I couldn't really do anything."

There was only one thing for it: find a new sport. Little did she know that within eight months of sitting in a canoe for the first time, she would be heading for a World Championships.

Cresswell started riding when she was three, introduced to the sport by her mum, who was "horsey" but "doing low-level amateur stuff".

"I was the only child at primary school that was allowed a phone because I used to cycle from my primary school to the yard so I could start riding before my mum came home from work," she says.

She got into eventing "properly" at 13 when she produced her own young pony from beginners level to eventually representing Great Britain at three European championships.

She glances at the medals on her wall, saying: "One gold and two team silvers... so that sort of sparked the whole eventing career."

Then came the leap of faith from her parents - "much to my poor brother's trauma who was not horsey in any way" and was suddenly now sharing a caravan with his older sister - and Cresswell began running the business of riding and competing horses for other people and coaching.

Since her accident, she has not been back on a horse. Nor does she intend to.

"Because I'd done it so seriously and to such a high level that every day was about perfecting my technique and being better, I think, to get back on and not be able to do that physically, but also not even feel the horse underneath me, I think it would just be very disheartening for me," she says.

Instead, she coaches, which she says has helped her with what has turned out - surprisingly to her - the thing she would miss the most about pre-accident life.

"[What I miss] is literally just having the horse on the yard, to just go and like say 'hello' to them over the stable," she says. "And that comes from somebody who was so busy that I didn't really have loads of time to do that anyway."

The coaching is one of the new parts of the family business, which has had to change since her accident.

"The business is basically having to diversify, which is still very much an ongoing process," she says.

"My parents had given up so much to build something that allowed me to do the sport. It wasn't like we were at home and I left home and did this - they were very invested as well. So it's kind of affected everybody from that side of things."

Cresswell had been beginning to make her mark at senior level when she was competing at Bramham Horse Trials on 8 June, 2024.

Three fences before the end of her under-25 cross-country round, she came off her horse Vivendi Hero.

"I remember all of it because I didn't even get knocked out," she says. "[It was] just a freak accident.

"I just landed on the back of my head and unfortunately broke my back at T4 level - so chest level - and basically as soon as I fell, instantly knew I couldn't feel my legs."

She remembers an "awful" 45-minute ambulance ride to Leeds General Infirmary, where she had emergency surgery.

At that point, she wondered whether the damage would be permanent, because only couple of weeks previously she had been chatting to a friend - Olympic silver medallist Nicola Wilson - who had broken her neck in a fall.

"She said, 'when I fell, I couldn't feel my arm for 20 minutes, and then my feeling came back'. So when I had my accident, I had this really weird thing, like I just thought, 'oh, it's fine, it'll be 20 minutes, and my feeling will come back'," she says.

Wilson, who visited Cresswell in intensive care, regained her feeling in her legs in three or four weeks.

"So I have this really weird thing because then I was sort of waiting for three to four weeks as if I was going to get feeling back," says Cresswell, who was moved to a spinal unit in Wakefield.

"It was probably not until about six weeks that the realisation really hits... that actually this wasn't going to be the outcome that I had hoped for."

Cresswell was bedbound for six weeks in what she calls her "hotel room", a private room in the hospital where the wall was covered in get-well-soon cards.

Even then, she kept busy as the physios would give her some weights she could use for her arms.

"They were tiny, but in my head, it was a principle of having something to do every day," she says.

One of the first parts of rehab was learning to sit up again.

"With a spinal injury your blood pressure gets really lowered. So I couldn't sit up in a wheelchair for longer than about five minutes without feeling faint," says Cresswell.

Then there were things like putting on socks or tying up her hair, although even by the time she left hospital she still could not do the latter while sitting up because she did not have any core strength or balance.

She remembers her timetable at the unit - official physio was 2pm til 3pm but she would be at the gym when it opened at 1pm, having also been at the physio room at 10am when that opened.

She was determined to keep busy - and creative about how to make that happen.

Take, for example, when she was told that it would take too many people to help her swim.

"Instead of saying anything, I just used to say OK, that's fine, but can I come and sit and watch? So, I was basically just making myself known by the swimming pool," says Cresswell, who credits her athlete's mindset for her drive and ability to take positives from every situation.

"So, I went for two weeks. I sat and watched these other people in the physios do swimming.

"And funnily enough, by the third week, they thought, 'we're going to have to let her go in the swimming pool now because she's just going to annoy us otherwise'."

It turned out, water was going to become a huge part of her life.

Around a week before she left the spinal unit, Cresswell attended the Spinal Games at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, which is for patients with spinal injuries who are either still in hospital or within a year post-accident, and is an opportunity to try different sports over four days.

"I got six out of six bull's eyes and won the archery out of 110 people," she says.

"It was a great stepping stone to coming home. And I think I kind of held on to that when I came home initially because the first while was really tough at home."

She left hospital on 8 October and by December had started wheelchair racing, going on to race 10Ks and a half-marathon, also doing wheelchair tennis and basketball.

"I was worried I would never find a sport that I wanted to put my whole energy into," she says. "I think I knew that horses were my hobby that got to turn into my sport and my career and lifestyle so I didn't know if that would be possible to find something like that."

Cresswell had got chatting to Olympic canoe athlete Deborah Kerr at an event run by the Women's Sport Trust charity who had told her to "have a go".

So, on 23 December last year, she did. Winter was "not the time to start a water sport" and she was "not a natural".

"My coach was too scared to let me off the bank in case I capsized," she laughs. "And that probably stayed, I don't think I left the bank for about a month."

A one-off taster session turned into twice a week and then eventually five times a week on the water. Four-hour training sessions, plus gym work three days a week.

One of the biggest challenges has been staying upright.

"I don't have any feedback of any part of my body if I am losing balance," she explains. "So I'm strapped into a seat because I've got no core function, but I can't actually feel that seat. So I basically feel like I'm floating.

"So my only thing I've got to know if I've lost balance is my head and my eyes. So that took a while to start to hone in and they always say, deaf people hear better than anybody else, don't they? And I think it's a bit the same.

"It's like, I've now tuned into how to balance myself without the use of the rest of my body. But I'd say the balance aspect is a big part of it alongside the technical, constant skill-based stuff that needs to be improved."

It is the technical aspect that she thinks has similarities to equestrian and which is why she thinks she enjoys it so much.

Her progress has been rapid, by anyone's standards. Not least her own.

"World Championships was definitely not the plan. It was a quiet goal after a while that if I could get the time, I might be able to go," says Cresswell, who alongside training is also doing media work.

"The time I needed to achieve was, I think, one minute 26 seconds. And anyway, I'm now down to one minute 18. So I've kind of over-achieved on that one, which has just been through repetition, practise, finding new ways to do things."

She has been selected to represent Great Britain at this month's Canoe Sprint and Para-Canoe World Championships in Poznan, Poland.

Having only ever raced once before in the UK her aims are modest.

"Honestly, stay up and get through the start and finish line," she says, explaining that she capsized before the start of a race she was due to do in April.

It is more about getting an international classification - which involves a series of medical tests to assess an athlete's impairment and demonstrating how much of your body you can use when paddling - so that she can be eligible to earn points at events that can lead to qualification for the 2028 Paralympics in Los Angeles.

Could she have pictured this when she was in hospital?

"I certainly wouldn't have imagined I was going to do para-canoe - I didn't even know [that] was a sport when I was in hospital," says Cresswell, who will compete in the VL1 (a canoe with a support float) and KL1 (kayak).

"But to be honest, I think what actually is more kind of crazy in my head is I couldn't even imagine January me doing this."

articles.title: Man United’s Fernandes, City’s Shaw named PFA Players of the Year
articles.summary: Fernandes rewarded for an outstanding season with a record number of assists in the league; Shaw builds on league win and Golden Boot.
articles.body:
Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes was crowned the Professional Footballers’ Association (PFA) Player of the Year, while Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw scooped the Women’s award for the second time.

The award wins on Tuesday highlighted the individual brilliance of both players, with contrasting fortunes for their respective teams during the season.

Portuguese international Fernandes broke the Premier League assists record during an outstanding 2025–26 season, setting up 21 goals as he surpassed Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne’s previous mark.

The 31-year-old also scored nine times as United overcame a poor start to finish third in the Premier League under Michael Carrick and earned a return to the Champions League.

Fernandes also won the Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year award in May.

“It is obviously a very proud moment. They are the ones you go on the pitch against, and it’s probably not easy to vote for someone you play against, so it is a very good moment,” said Fernandes.

Shaw was rewarded for scoring 21 goals on the way to a third straight Golden Boot and securing City’s first Women’s Super League title in a decade.

City also saw further success as Nico O’Reilly was named Men’s Young Player of the Year.

The 21-year-old scored twice in the League Cup final as City beat Arsenal and was part of the side that also won the FA Cup last season.

“I’m very proud of the season I had,” said the England international. “I won two trophies with my club and managed to play at the World Cup with my country. I’m over the moon with how it turned out.”

O’Reilly was joined by City teammates Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Antoine Semenyo in the Team of the Year.

Champions Arsenal had five representatives in David Raya, Gabriel, William Saliba, Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice, with Fernandes and Brentford’s Igor Thiago completing the XI.

articles.title: Roberto Gómez: "Lo que han hecho Laporta y Deco ha sido impresentable"
articles.standfirst: El periodista carga en La Tribu contra el Barcelona por el caso Julián Álvarez, critica con dureza el 'Tiempo de revisión' y analiza el regreso de Mourinho al Real Madrid
articles.summary: El periodista carga en La Tribu contra el Barcelona por el caso Julián Álvarez, critica con dureza el 'Tiempo de revisión' y analiza el regreso de Mourinho al Real Madrid
articles.body: Roberto Gómez pasó este miércoles por La Tribu, con Javi Amaro, y dejó una intervención cargada de asuntos. El periodista fue especialmente duro con el Barcelona por su actuación alrededor de Julián Álvarez, pero también mostró su rechazo al 'Tiempo de revisión' y analizó el regreso de Mourinho al banquillo del Real Madrid. El futuro de Julián Álvarez fue uno de los asuntos centrales. Gómez cargó directamente contra el Barcelona por sus movimientos alrededor del futbolista. "Lo que está haciendo el Barcelona es un chantaje brutal, que pare ya", aseguró. El periodista señaló directamente a los responsables de la entidad azulgrana: "Basta ya, lo que ha sido impresentable y no tiene nombre es lo que ha hecho Laporta y lo que ha hecho Deco". Y cerró su reflexión con otra afirmación contundente: "Yo creo que lo que ha intentado el Barcelona es asaltar, literalmente, el Atlético de Madrid. Esto no se puede consentir". Antes de abordar el mercado, Roberto Gómez había mostrado su enorme enfado con el 'Tiempo de revisión'. La expulsión de Yuri fue uno de los ejemplos que utilizó para explicar su postura. "Que lo quiten. Yo soy el Athletic y ahora mismo me voy al juzgado de guardia. Y digo: 'Señores, ¿qué ha pasado aquí? ¿Pero esto qué es? Esto es una vergüenza. Que lo quiten ya". Gómez considera que el sistema puede convertirse en un problema durante toda la temporada: "Que no haya otra jornada más de revisión. Es una manipulación total". También recordó otras decisiones arbitrales que considera polémicas: "Hay dos acciones en Sevilla en el primer partido que son brutales y quedan despachadas de una manera impresentable. Lo mismo que la acción de la patada de Cala a Vinicius". El periodista terminó siendo categórico: "¿Qué les parece el sistema de revisión? Es una vergüenza. Es una vergüenza". También reclamó que los árbitros se centren en su preparación: "Que se dediquen, en lugar de revisar, que se dediquen a prepararse bien, a concienciarse bien". Otro de los grandes asuntos de la intervención fue el regreso de Mourinho al Bernabéu. Roberto Gómez elogió al portugués y explicó cómo interpreta su vuelta: "Vuelve a un hábitat en donde él ha estado muy a gusto durante los años que estuvo en el Bernabéu. Ha vuelto, indudablemente, con una tranquilidad, probablemente por los años, por la experiencia y por saber dónde vuelve". Eso sí, considera que el portugués llega con la máxima exigencia. "El Real Madrid lo ha traído para que gane", afirmó. Y fue más allá al enumerar los objetivos: "Tiene la obligación de ganar, y de ganar Champions, Liga y Copa". Roberto Gómez también respaldó públicamente la postura del entrenador con Vinicius: "Me parece muy bien la protección que quiere tener sobre Vinicius". Según el periodista, el brasileño "se ha convertido en objetivo de muchísimas defensas" y existe "muy poca protección por parte de los árbitros". Por eso concluyó: "Esta protección que le quiere dar Mourinho desde un principio me parece tremendamente correcta".

articles.title: Brighton & Hove Albion sign Algerian left-back Jaouen Hadjam
articles.summary: The 23-year-old joins from Swiss champions Young Boys on a five-year deal, making him the third Algerian in the league.
articles.body:
Algerian defender Jaouen Hadjam has joined Brighton & Hove Albion from Swiss champions Young Boys for an undisclosed fee on a contract until 2031, the Premier League club has confirmed.

Brighton announced the signing on Tuesday with a video showing the left-back sipping mint tea in a cafe.

Hadjam joins Manchester City’s Rayan Ait-Nouri and Hull City’s Mohamed El Bachir Belloumi as Algerian internationals playing in the Premier League.

Former Leicester City and Manchester City winger Riyad Mahrez is arguably the most famous and successful Algerian to have played in the league.

The Paris-born player represented France at youth level before switching allegiance to Algeria in 2023. He has earned 21 caps for his country.

Hadjam, 23, made 98 appearances for Young Boys in all competitions after joining the Swiss side from Ligue 1 club Nantes in 2024. He played in Paris Saint-Germain’s youth academy.

He was part of Algeria’s squad at the FIFA World Cup 2026, where he played in three of the team’s four matches.

Brighton started their league campaign by beating Europa League holders Aston Villa 4-0 on Sunday.

articles.title: Raúl Fuentes desvela los planes del Barça para el final de mercado: Julián Álvarez y varias salidas
articles.standfirst: El periodista explicó la situación de la plantilla azulgrana y aseguró que Casadó y Fort saldrán, mientras que el club estaría dispuesto a estudiar una buena oferta por Koundé.
articles.summary: El periodista explicó la situación de la plantilla azulgrana y aseguró que Casadó y Fort saldrán, mientras que el club estaría dispuesto a estudiar una buena oferta por Koundé.
articles.body: El Barcelona afronta los últimos días del mercado con varios frentes abiertos. Raúl Fuentes explicó en La Tribu, patrocinada por Sportium durante esta temporada, la hoja de ruta azulgrana para este tramo final, tanto en el capítulo de llegadas como en el de salidas. Una planificación en la que Julián Álvarez continúa siendo el gran objetivo para la delantera. Según explicó Fuentes, la postura del Barça respecto al '9' está muy definida después de la reunión que mantuvieron Laporta, Deco, Flick y Bojan: "La estrategia a seguir es, en cuanto al delantero centro, o viene Julián Álvarez o no viene nadie, como mínimo hasta el mercado invernal". El periodista señaló además los esfuerzos que estaría realizando el delantero para intentar vestir de azulgrana: "Más de lo que está haciendo Julián por querer vestir la camiseta del Barça no se puede hacer más, entonces el Barça no lo va a dejar tirado hasta que se cierre el mercado". Fuentes también apuntó a la posibilidad de un nuevo movimiento económico: "Yo creo que el Barça puede subir un poco la oferta de los 100 millones que presentó a final del mes de junio". El mercado de salidas también promete movimiento durante los próximos días. En este sentido, Fuentes fue contundente con dos futbolistas de la plantilla: "Casadó y Fort se van a ir". Pero no serían los únicos nombres a seguir. El periodista puso encima de la mesa otras dos situaciones: "Luego también hay un par de patatas calientes, la patata caliente de Alejandro Balde después de dejarle fuera de la lista el domingo en Elche, y el tema de Koundé, que es un tema diferente al de Balde". Especialmente significativo es el caso de Jules Koundé. Fuentes aseguró que el francés cuenta con mercado en la Premier y explicó su situación actual en los planes de Hansi Flick: "Es un jugador que tiene buen mercado en Inglaterra". Además, añadió: "Ahora Koundé para Flick es, digamos, el tercer central, no lo ve de lateral porque el lateral es Eric García". Una situación que podría provocar que el Barça escuchase propuestas por el francés en este tramo final del mercado: "Si llega algo interesante por Koundé, pues el club se lo miraría con buenos ojos". La portería es otro de los asuntos que tiene que resolver el Barcelona. David Bernabéu habló de la llegada de Livakovic y de la posibilidad de que finalmente permanezca esta misma temporada en el equipo: "Yo creo que será para esta". El periodista fue especialmente crítico con el estado físico de Szczesny: "Está muy mal físicamente. Tú le ves la estampa y parece un jugador o un portero de Tercera Catalana". También reconoció, sin embargo, el peso que tiene el polaco dentro del vestuario: "Para Flick en el vestuario es una pieza importante". Bernabéu aseguró haber hablado con jugadores de la plantilla sobre el papel del guardameta: "Ellos te dicen que están encantados con él, que hace mucho grupo, que les da muchos consejos". La situación podría terminar influyendo en los planes con Livakovic. Según explicó David Bernabéu, "el Barça le ha firmado cuatro años a Livakovic y la idea inicial era cederle una temporada para recuperarle al final del contrato del polaco", aunque considera que el escenario ha cambiado y que el guardameta podría quedarse ya en la plantilla azulgrana.

articles.title: Bodo return to Champions League, Azerbaijan’s Sabah deny Israeli Beer-Sheva
articles.summary: Scottish champions Celtic thumped by LASK as Sabah knock out Hapoel Beer-Sheva with a late goal in the qualifying round.
articles.body:
The UEFA Champions League’s feel-good story, Bodo/Glimt, are back for a second season, joined by LASK of Austria and debutants Sabah of Azerbaijan.

Bodo/Glimt eased through the second leg of their qualifying playoff on Tuesday against NEC Nijmegen, and Sabah, a club formed eight years ago, denied Israeli Premier League champions Hapoel Beer-Sheva in extra time after a last-gasp goal in regulation time levelled the aggregate score.

LASK seemed all but out after a half-hour on Tuesday, trailing 4-0 on aggregate to Celtic, who had taken a three-goal win from the first leg last week in Glasgow.

Still, LASK had already rained scoring chances on Celtic’s goal even before falling further behind, and somehow only retrieved three goals of the deficit when the clock passed 90 minutes.

Then Florian Flecker’s close-range header forced extra time, during which the Scottish champions continued to implode.

A fifth unanswered goal for LASK came in the 109th minute by Samuel Adeniran, who then had a penalty saved as the score stayed 5-1 on the night and 5-4 on aggregate. Celtic drop into the second-tier Europa League.

Four more playoff second-leg games on Wednesday will confirm the final entries in the 36-team main phase. The draw for those games is made on Thursday in Monaco.

Bodo/Glimt’s storied series of wins in January and February against Manchester City, Atletico Madrid and Inter Milan makes the Norwegian fishing town team seem like Champions League veterans compared with Sabah.

On Tuesday, Dutch newcomers NEC lost 3-0 as the latest visitors to the Arctic Circle suffered on the artificial turf inside Glimt’s tiny Aspmyra Stadium. The aggregate score was 6-1.

Any hope of a comeback ended after three minutes when NEC goalkeeper Gonzalo Crettaz handled the ball outside his penalty area and was sent off.

Sabah secure debut with late win over Hapoel Beer-Sheva

Sabah football club was created in September 2017 and, exactly nine years later, will debut in the Champions League’s main competition after a dramatic qualifying playoff win, joining Italy’s Como as Champions League newcomers.

Sabah were just seconds from elimination against the Israeli champions, who won the first leg 2-1 last week, when substitute Tellur Mutallimov scored in the last minute of stoppage time to force extra time.

Sabah’s Gabon striker Orphe Mbina then scored with a header in the 101st minute, and Joy-Lance Mickels added on in the 115th to make it 5-2 in the second leg and 6-4 on aggregate.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva finished with nine players after leading 4-2 on aggregate in the 61st minute, when right-back Guy Mizrahi scored with a shot from outside the penalty area.

Defender Djibril Diop and midfielder Eliel Peretz were both shown second yellow cards in extra time.

No Israeli team has played in the main Champions League since November 2022, when Maccabi Haifa finished last in a group with Benfica, Paris Saint-Germain and Juventus.

Israeli teams participate in European competitions as the national football federation is a member of UEFA. It joined the European confederation in 1994 after its expulsion from the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) in 1973, following the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.

articles.title: Omar Marmoush transfer news: Tottenham agree deal to sign Man City forward on loan with £60m obligation to buy
articles.summary: Tottenham have agreed a deal to sign Omar Marmoush from Man City; Spurs are set to sign the forward on an initial loan move with a £60m obligation to buy; Marmoush is set to undergo a medical ahead of following former City team-mate Savio to Spurs, who signed on Tuesday
articles.body:
The Egypt forward is set for a medical ahead of completing an initial loan move with a £60m obligation to buy him permanently.

Sky Sports News understands the fee is broken up into a £50m guaranteed payment plus £10m in bonuses.

Eintracht Frankfurt, who sold Marmoush to City in January 2025, do not have a sell-on clause, contrary to reports.

The German club received their desired guaranteed fee at the time, plus additional bonuses.

There were also very few instalments, meaning all payment obligations to Frankfurt have been fulfilled by City.

Marmoush now looks set to follow former City teammate Savio to join Roberto De Zerbi's squad, after the Brazil winger completed an £85m move to Spurs on Tuesday .

Speaking ahead of Tottenham facing Charlton in the second round of the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, live on Sky Sports , De Zerbi said Spurs would continue to spend in the transfer market.

The £85m signing of Savio took their spend to over £300m for the summer transfer window after already signing Sandro Tonali , Mateus Fernandes and Jan Paul van Hecke. Andy Robertson and Marcos Senesi have also arrived on free transfers.

"I don't feel pressure about the transfer market. If I can, I want to spend more money again without problems, because the other teams don't spend anything different," De Zerbi said.

"I feel pressure because I am working in one of the best clubs in the world and I would like to help this club to compete to win the titles.

"I don't know [whether] this season or next season, but, in the end, it's my big target, my personal target.

"We have nothing less than the other big clubs in the Premier League, especially now, in my time. We are moving very well in the transfer market and why not?

"I can't understand why Tottenham can't compete with Liverpool, Manchester City, Chelsea, Arsenal. I don't understand why Tottenham can't spend the same money as Chelsea, Liverpool."

articles.title: Infantino has no future at FIFA, says European Leagues chief
articles.summary: Claudius Schaefer insists the influence of the FIFA president has ‘grown from year to year’.
articles.body:
Gianni Infantino ⁠cannot have a future at FIFA, European Leagues president Claudius Schaefer has said, stressing the importance of reforming world football’s governing body and the responsibilities of its boss.

In ⁠an interview with The Athletic published on Wednesday, Schaefer said European Leagues, which represents 53 professional men’s and women’s football leagues, was deeply concerned about Infantino’s leadership.

“We question his suitability to continue as ⁠president. Here in Switzerland, we’ve had a close view of FIFA, and it seems that the influence of the president has grown from year to year,” he added.

“Major decisions are taken without meaningful consultation with stakeholders who will be affected.”

Schaefer’s comments come amid a bitter conflict among governing bodies, prompted by FIFA’s now-abandoned ‌proposal to sell off a slice of the World Cup’s commercial rights.

Infantino is under pressure from three confederations to resign, including Europe’s UEFA, Asia’s AFC and CONCACAF, which represents North and Central America and the Caribbean. The sport’s regional bodies have also discussed a potential vote of no confidence against the FIFA chief.

Concerns have been raised over the inaugural FIFA peace prize awarded to United States President Donald Trump in December and the ⁠overturning of a ban for USA forward Folarin Balogun during this year’s World ⁠Cup following a call from the Republican leader.

“FIFA is an association under Swiss law and in this association you have rules. The president and the board members have to perform their duties with care. This is a legal matter,” Schaefer said.

“If you take ⁠such a decision [as the peace prize] without even informing the council, that, in my view, is a breach of law. And then, during the World ⁠Cup, we all know about the red card issue.

“It was a ⁠real scandal. I can’t ever recall a political intervention of this kind relating to a sporting matter. Such acts call the integrity of the game into question. That’s why there is no future at FIFA for Infantino. There can’t be.”

Infantino will be seeking ‌re-election for a fourth term next year and will likely face stiff opposition, but Schaefer said it was more important to redefine the role of FIFA president than it was to get someone else ‌into ‌office.

“For us, getting these reforms is the most important task, and they can only happen with another president,” he added.
